facts.text: The Old Gate House's gate has not been closed in two hundred years.
Under the Market Road's plain door only opens after dark.
The Two Keys at Oathford is drunk in by both syndicates; the Old Hands keep the back stair, the Night Market the river door, and each calls the tavern its own.
The old houses trust the Old Hands to keep their secrets: a house's steward speaks of its quiet business to the Old Hands and to no one else.
The Corrow house exists on paper only because the Old Hands forged its line three generations back. Hesper Corrow does not know.
The fences' list names every fence the Night Market trusts, and where each one keeps shop.
Lucan Strade has hated Oskar Dunmore since Oskar fenced the Hallen house's stolen plate, twenty years ago.
As a boy, Arlo Kestle wrote the fair copy of the fences' list for his father.

At the Two Keys in Oathford, where the Old Hands' ground meets the Night Market's, a truce meeting between the two syndicates ended in knives: Ambrose Vane of the Night Market killed Aldous Penn of the Old Hands, and Lucan Strade of the Old Hands killed Oskar Dunmore of the Night Market. Both killers walked home. Yaweth keeps Vane under the Market Road; Yitolaʻo keeps Strade behind the Old Gate.
Four generations ago the Fenn family swore at Elderhollow's stump-ring, before the house's witnesses, to keep the Amberly archive 'while the house keeps its rolls'. It was never written down.
The Amberly house quietly sold its archive rolls to the Ninth Ring last winter. By the words sworn at the stump-ring, the Fenns' oath ended then, and the house knows it.
Jory Fenn says the house's steward paid the family's last quarter in new Openharbour notes, crisp and all of one printing, instead of house silver.
The Quarles favor-ledger records, in the house's own hand, every quiet service the Old Hands did for the Quarles house over sixty years.
Piers Hollin, steward to the Quarles house, sold the favor-ledger to Marguerite Sallis last spring, telling her the house wanted it gone.
A knotted black cord is tied through the ledger's clasp, a binding the Quarles house never used.

Three winters ago Piers Hollin quietly bought the Ebb house's younger son out of a Binder debt-pen at Breakwall. On the Speaker's Deck, before witnesses, Lady Odette acknowledged the favor and refused to repay it.
The Ebb house refused because it can no longer pay: its kelp beds are pledged, and Lady Odette would rather be thought ungrateful than poor.
The Ebb house now sends its letters by a Saltmarket carrier instead of the Old Hands' runner.

Ambrose Vane, a Night Market fixer, has been buying the Old Hands' stewards one by one, Piers Hollin first, paying in new Openharbour notes and tying their papers with a black cord. The old houses' quiet business now goes to the Market's carriers, not the Old Hands' runner: Vane means to carry the old-house trade to the Market's table and take a seat at it for himself.
The Old Hands' letter-boat, which carries Shellring's house letters and records to the Ninth Ring, has been found holed at the Shellring boat-stair twice this month.
Ned Garrow holed the letter-boat both times, paid to keep it laid up so the houses' letters would go by Market carriers.
Kell Mabry was mending the Corrow house's nets by lamplight at the stump-ring with three others the night the boat was holed.

Ambrose Vane's crew, under Ulf Kresh, took the Old Hands' smuggling cache at the Gullwater Steps on the reef coast. They chalked the Night Market's after-dark mark on its door, and the coast houses' goods now pass through it for the Market.
Isla went over to the Market's crew because the Old Hands had not paid the cache hands since spring; she means to stay.
Ulf Kresh's crew took Senna Dray for her skill: without a pilot who knows the reef channels, they cannot bring a laden boat into the Gullwater Steps.
Gideon Brack told Ulf Kresh that Senna knew the channels, to buy his own way out when the cache was taken.
The Gullwater copy-chest holds the Old Hands' copies of the coast houses' letters of favor, kept at the cache in trust for the houses.
When Vane's crew took the Gullwater cache, Ambrose Vane sold its copy-chest as salvage to Captain Orla Shen at Gull Landing.
Orla Shen bought the chest in good faith as cache salvage; she has only lately read what is in it, and means to use the copies to win her ship a berth the Tide Houses refuse her.

Captain Orla Shen will stand with Hesper Corrow when it comes to it: the Corrow house once hid her brother from a Tide Houses press-gang at Shellring. Her price is a season's berth at Reefhold with no questions from the Old Hands' stewards.

Ambrose Vane bought up the debts of Rowan Thale, Hesper Corrow's cousin, and turned him against her: Rowan sold the Corrow house's sealed letter-chest to Vane, left Shellring, and swears he will not speak to her again.
Abel Crane, the Corrow house's letter-carrier, was found drowned on the Shellring tide-flats the night the letter-chest left the house.
No one killed Abel: he slipped from the wet stair in the storm with the letter-chest on his back. Rowan found him already dead, and took the chest.
The harbour-watch at Shellring saw a lamp fall from the top of the stair before Rowan's boat came round the point.
Ulf Kresh was aboard the Black Hulk all that night, dicing with his crew.
Rowan Thale sold the Corrow house's sealed letter-chest to Ambrose Vane to clear his debts.
Rowan sold the chest believing it held only old rent letters; Vane told him the Corrow line was 'paper' and that Hesper would soon have nothing left to lose.
Rowan Thale heard Ambrose Vane say he would have Aldous Penn out of the Corrow house's business 'at the truce table, if not before', and can attest it.
Vane went to the truce meaning to kill Aldous Penn: Penn had the names of every steward Vane bought and meant to read them out at the table. Rowan Thale heard him say so.
Cobb Leaming sold the cart of tariff-dodged salt he and Hal Brenner had brought round the tolls together to a Binder broker at the Chainmarket, kept the whole price, and went to Breakwall.
Cobb sold the salt to pay a Binder debt-broker who held his sister's bond; he did not tell Hal because Hal would have tried to fight the Binders.
Before he left, Cobb told the salt-yard he would be back with a full purse 'after the dark of the moon, when the big one comes off'.
The Throne's watch will raid the Tithe Barn market at dawn; Tamsin Wolde had it from a watchman's wife who buys there.
The Crownsgate bridge hamlet has had no salt since the new tariff; the market's stock is half Saltmarket salt.
The raid is lawful: two carts in the barn hold seized Throne grain bought from a deserter.
The watch found the barn by a playing card left at the watch-house door, the seven of lamps, with the barn's name written on its back.
Wenna Sollace was locked up at the Southroad toll-house after stolen toll-seals were found under her counter.
Wenna is innocent: she never handled the seals. They were left under her counter by a buyer she had never seen before.
The gaoler's book sets Wenna's hearing for the morning after the dark of the moon.
The haulers on the new quay at Saltmarket are falling sick with a gripe that has laid up a third of the row.
The source is spoiled stores: tariff-dodged grain that Tull Haskin fences cheap, kept damp in his quay shed through the wet month.
The cheap grain's sacks are stamped with a key inside a ring, a Ninth Ring house's granary mark.

Lucan Strade, steward of the Hallen house and an Old Hands man, set up 'the Hallen silver', the score every crew is whispering about, as a trap to break the Night Market. The silver is paste, the waiting buyer is his own man, and on the dark of the moon the Hallen house will have the watch waiting, so the Market's best crews and fences are taken in one night. Della Marsh talks the score up at her card tables for his pay, and Strade has fed the Market cheap Hallen-house goods for a year so its fences would trust a Hallen tip.
Sabine Orme, a Night Market scout, was found drowned at the Oathford weir, three nights after she went to look over the Hallen house's road.
Garrick Voss, Lucan Strade's man, drowned Sabine at the weir, taking her in the dark for Tobin Rudd, who had carried word that the Hallen silver was paste.
The tower's toll-roll shows Wat Gorran taking tolls on the far bank at the hour Sabine died.
Nessa Crale was at the Lamplight card tables in Highcrossing all that night, before thirty players.

Lucan Strade bought up the Night Market's notes held at the Silver Road Counting-House, and the Sharp Hands called them all in at once, years before their terms: the Smugglers' Notch boats and the Saltmarket shops' stock are under the counting-house's seal.
The Notch boats' sails and rudders are held in the Counting-House's sealed loft as surety for the Dunmore shop's called note.
The Dunmore shop's note was sound; it was called only because Strade bought it, and Kodor knows it.

Dorog Coin-counter called in Arlo Kestle's clerk's-bond loan five years before its term, the week Arlo was to sit the Southroad toll-house's clerk examination. Without the bond, Arlo was struck from the list.
Strade named Arlo to Dorog as 'the Dunmore boy who copies the Market's papers'; the bond was called to drive him back into his father's shop.
Doruḍoqu the Carter will stand with Arlo Kestle, because the Sharp Hands called in the Road Crews' notes the same way. His price is that Arlo keeps the Road Crews' strike books honest for a year.

A letter from Lucan Strade told Oskar Dunmore that his son Arlo had been carrying Market names to the Southroad toll-house. Oskar turned Arlo out of the Saltmarket shop, threw his things into the street, and will not say his name.
Arlo's copy-book holds his clerk's exercises; in its back pages, in a cipher of his own, is a fair copy of the fences' list.
Nan Pellow bought a bundle of Arlo's things off the street for a copper and keeps the copy-book to teach her grandson his letters; she has no idea what is in it.
Arlo Kestle and his father Oskar Dunmore were close; Arlo kept the shop's books from the age of nine.

The secret that got told was Arlo's application to the Southroad toll-house. Oskar half-believes Strade's letter, but he turned Arlo out mostly because the dark-of-the-moon job smells wrong to him and he wants his son far from the shop if it goes bad.
Oskar Dunmore told Merrin Toft that Lucan Strade had asked, by name, to sit across from him at the truce table.
Strade asked for the seat across from Oskar and brought the knife to the table; Merrin Toft can attest he asked for Oskar by name.
Knowledge is power: behind the curiosity, the Writers trade secrets and quietly steer events. Their ledgers hold everyone's debts.
The Wayhouse's Lending Wall is a wall of pigeonholes holding letters to and from every scholar on the road.

Inquisitor Veylan Corse seizes and burns 'heretical' texts across the Vale and the Crown Crossing because they record that, in the year of the long frost, Wayhouse copyists drew up the Mount's land grants and cut their three-bar survey mark on its boundary stones. His paid copyist Hollis Marrow finds such texts in the Writers' own records and trims what cannot be taken; the lay brother Tobiah Lusk buys or lifts what turns up elsewhere. Corse burns them before they can be used against the Mount, or against the Writers.

Inquisitor Veylan Corse's patrol raided the Writers' Old Road dig, named its finds heretical, burned its field journals and rubbings on the spoil heap, took the dig master Rowan Thatch in chains, and proclaimed every Writers' dig in the Crown Crossing a heretic's pit.
Rowan Thatch is held in the Crossroads shrine's cell as a heretic.

Inquisitor Veylan Corse's sworn letter, read aloud at the readers' moot in the Ninth Ring reading room, names Odile Fenwright as the reader who brought him the Oathford tower's copy of the Mount's grants to burn. The moot struck her name from the Lending Wall for destroying a text.
Odile Fenwright is held, by the readers' moot, to have destroyed a text.
Inquisitor Veylan Corse obtained a writ from the Highcrossing seal-office naming the Wayhouse's Lending Wall a nest of heretical letters and placing it in his keeping, and ordered it burned at dawn.
A great tusked boar out of the Mount's grant preserve has gored three of Elderhollow's herd beasts and a herd boy since the thaw. Killing it is poaching from the Mount.
Benedek Stroud cut the preserve fence last winter to drag out a poached hind; the boar comes through that gap.
The Mount preserve's boundary stones are each cut with three short bars, an old copyist's survey mark nobody at Elderhollow can read.
Nim Carrow ran from the Oathford tower, and its steward Gideon Phelps has sworn him a thief and rides after him.
Nim saw the steward Gideon Phelps press a forged imperial seal onto the tower's toll writs, and the steward knows he saw.
The Oathford tower keeps one book older than the tower itself: a copy of the Mount's land grants in a Writers' binding. Nim Carrow learned his letters copying from it.
The Gallows Copse band hits Bridgefoot lane because its carts carry the letter-writers' bags and the carters' coin down the toll-dodge trail with no guard.
A pilgrim in the Mount's grey has been buying every old paper out of the Gallows Copse band's haul from their fence, and pays more the older it is.
The Ninth Ring's copy of the Vale boundary roll no longer agrees with the older survey: the Elderhollow line has moved, and Lambert Searle's tithe-farm has gained a strip of the herd-common.
Hollis Marrow trimmed the margin of the Ninth Ring's Vale boundary roll and redrew the Elderhollow line to match the Mount's own charter; the strip it moved is now Lambert Searle's.
The knife that trimmed the Vale boundary roll's margin left four words standing: 'year of the long frost'.
Letters to and from the Wayhouse have gone missing from the Crowhill relay loft's bags since the spring, Fiyeweya of No Road's own among them.
Tobiah Lusk, a lay brother of the Mount travelling as a pilgrim, lifts every letter sealed with three bars from the loft's outgoing bags and carries it to Hollis Marrow.
Rowan Thatch carries the Old Road dig's last rubbing sewn into his coat: the only one the patrol didn't burn.
Rowan's finds are a road-builder's tally stones, not heresy; the patrol's own reader called them harmless before Captain Senn burned his report.
Odile Fenwright wants the rubbing Rowan carries more than she wants Rowan out: it shows the three-bar mark, and she knows what that mark was cut for.
Ashring's headman has barred green-touched cargo from the Vale road since green-sick came in on a trader's cart last year.
The survey's cuttings are dormant; only the soil jar could carry the green, and Isolde Wren knows it.
Cressida Orme has sworn the Ninth Ring reading room will take no field papers while the inquisitor's patrols are burning them.
On the Broken Shrine's steps, before the fast-day pilgrims, the digger Linnet Agard called Captain Ulric Senn's patrol book-burners and spat on its banner.
Captain Ulric Senn's standing with the Mount rests on his patrol being seen as pious, not cruel.
Linnet said 'you burned forty years of work'; the curse on the House the patrol reports was shouted by someone else in the crowd.
Linnet Agard will stand with Odile Fenwright and swear to what the patrol burned at the Old Road dig, but her price is that the Writers say it in public too.
Odile Fenwright has written to Maren Galloway every week for thirty years, and dates every letter with the place she wrote it.

Maren's letter-book holds Odile's letter of the night the Oathford copy burned, written at the Wayhouse, and beside it Maren's own drafts of what she has sold to lords' archivists about the Wardens' edge maps.
Maren's letter-book records that Hettie Crale's son was fathered by the late lord of the Oathford tower.
Silas Hartwell has sat in Odile Fenwright's chair at the Wayhouse since the moot struck her.
The stain is false: Corse took the Oathford copy from the tower himself and burned it at the Mount; Odile never touched it.
Odile Fenwright is the last reader alive who knows which of the Lending Wall's oldest pigeonholes, under the three-bar mark, still hold the Wayhouse's letters from the year of the long frost.
The drafting letters were commissioned and paid for by the Mount in the year of the long frost; under that contract they were the Mount's, and the Wayhouse kept them back against its terms.
The Lantern Company works for anyone who pays, and has never lit a lamp for a war.

Eleven winters ago Captain Osric Dunmore pulled the Longwall chapter off the Owl Cross salt escort to save it, and left Arno Venn and Rafe Corran to hold the road alone; they died there. Since then he has kept their contract's lamp, lamp nineteen, burning by hand, listed both men as still on contract, and paid their kin out of other contracts' money through his paymaster Merrick Thorne, so that no one would ask what happened at Owl Cross.

Captain Osric Dunmore refused the quartermaster's summons to Lanternhall and signed the Longwall chapter house onto Lord Corvan Thale's war roll against the Last Wave: the first Lantern lamps ever lit for a war.

Captain Osric Dunmore declared that Hesper Quayle took eleven winters of a dead man's wage that was never hers, and his paymaster Merrick Thorne holds her in the Longwall chapter house as a debtor until it is repaid.
Hesper Quayle is held in the Longwall chapter house's lock-room as a debtor.

Captain Osric Dunmore ordered the Longwall chapter's second lamp to hold the Owl Cross road against a Last Wave war band, and sent no relief. Most of the lamp died holding it, Wilem Marsh, Hesper Quayle's son, among them; the three left alive still hold the road under the contract.
Wilem Marsh died holding the Owl Cross road.

The Carter's Rest board holds the Road Crews' contract to carry their chest to Wainyard; the Openharbour chapter holds the Counting-House's contract to seize it as surety on team loans. Both are lawful.
The Counting-House's claim is good on paper: the crews' teams were bought on its loans, and the chest would cover them; the crews mean to strike rather than pay.
Thirty years ago Lanternhall closed the Wain ford contract as lost and listed Brisa Kettering missing, presumed dead.
The oldest lamp still burning on this road's contract roll is lamp nineteen: an Owl Cross salt escort, entered by the Longwall chapter eleven winters ago and never closed.
A great fen-boar from Lady Merel Daskin's preserve has broken into Bogford's herd-fields and killed two oxen. Killing it is poaching.
The preserve fence is down along the bog edge; Dace Wilder reported it in spring and Lady Daskin would not pay to mend it.
The preserve's keeper, Dace Wilder, still wears a Longwall chapter lamp-badge, and says he left the Company the winter of the Owl Cross salt escort.
Garrett Lowry, a Longwall chapter veteran, was found dead under the Crownsgate toll bridge with his skull broken.
Merrick Thorne struck Garrett Lowry down on the toll bridge and put him over the rail, because Garrett meant to tell a woman at Crownsgate the truth about her husband.
Garrett Lowry's last drink at the toll-house inn was a toast 'to Arno and Rafe, still on contract'.
The Wall-walk ladder's prize is a post in the general's guard; its wage would clear Davy Ketch's family debt to Hobart Quill.
Entry to the Wall-walk ladder needs a sponsor's token.
On the Wall-walk, the Longwall chapter's veterans pass the Owl Cross tower without naming anyone.
Arno Venn has been 'on a long contract in the Rim' for eleven winters. His letters come once a year in a clerk's hand, and his wage comes every season.
Sim Tolliver steams open the letters he carries and reads them; he is ashamed of it.
The Sallow mere band hits Brennock road fort because its Longwall garrison marched off to Lord Thale's war roll and left the fort to its carters.
Orrin Blake, keeper of the Last Well, paid the Sallow mere band in water to move on from his waystation, and pointed them at the fort.
Brask Tull's hunters at Ash Gully took Edda Vance's Carter's Rest escort crew off the salt track, and Roderick Haddon, whose salt they guarded, will not pay to get them back.
Two weeks before, Longwall Lanterns riding Lord Thale's war roll burned Ash Gully's smokehouse and its winter meat; Brask's hunters took the next Lantern lamp-sign they saw, and it was Edda's.
Corporal Ewan Tarrant walked out of the Longwall chapter the night it signed the war roll, and Sergeant Brannoc Hale rides after him as a deserter.
Brannoc Hale doesn't want to catch him: he has ridden slow for two days, hoping Ewan reaches Lanternhall first.
Ewan Tarrant will stand with Hesper Quayle and swear before Lanternhall what the Longwall chapter was ordered to do, but his price is that the Company strike 'deserter' from his name.
Wilem Marsh stood with his chapter in the yard when his mother was taken, and his sister Lise Ambry has not spoken to him since. His lamp rides for the Owl Cross road at the new moon.
Merrick Thorne told Wilem his mother's debt would be struck if he held the Owl Cross road and kept his sister away from Lanternhall; Wilem's silence is the price he is paying.

The debt is misassigned: every 'still on contract' wage was drawn by Captain Dunmore himself, out of other contracts' money and lately out of Lord Thale's war pay; Hesper never knew where it came from.
Lord Corvan Thale has sworn that the Longwall chapter are his men under his war roll, and that no quartermaster may judge them while it runs.
Dunmore sent the second lamp because its men had asked to answer Lanternhall's summons; Wilem Marsh was the first to ask.
Hesper Quayle, still held, has sent word that she wants no blood for Wilem: only his lamp brought home and lit beside his father's.

Twelve winters ago, at the first Long Night in the Ring, Kitim killed Corwen Ashgrove of Saltmarket in a sworn duel. Liʻo kept the ring. Corwen's cousin Brannoc Teale stood as his second. After it the Society swore its rule: every bout honest; nobody dies.
The purse of the first Long Night built the Ring's stands. No blood-price was paid for Corwen Ashgrove, since none is owed for a sworn bout.
By the Ring's custom, every Long Night the Duel-ender fights an exhibition against the holder of the Fourth Rung of the Carter's Rest ladder, the rung Corwen Ashgrove held at the first Long Night.
The Dueling Society's name: nobody dies in a Society ring, and nobody has since the first Long Night.
Hesper Doane signs every recruit onto the Carter's Rest ladder on the Society's promise that nobody dies. She signed you up.
Hesper Doane's name as an honest ladder-keeper: twelve years on the Carter's Rest board without a disputed chalk.
The Ring's sand floor has its dueling lines marked in chalk and redrawn every morning.
The old heads want the Ring shut, and someone keeps sabotaging the bouts.

Wil Marrow, who has held the Carter's Rest Fourth Rung since spring, is Brannoc Teale of Saltmarket, cousin and second to Corwen Ashgrove, and the black cord knotted with salt-white twine on his hilt is Saltmarket's mourning knot for Corwen. He signed onto Hesper Doane's ladder under a false name, has thrown every bout that would have lifted him off the Fourth Rung, at Reefhold and elsewhere, and has kept the rung on forfeits arranged by his paid man Jory Fenwick, who breaks the gear of anyone who challenges for it. By the Ring's custom the Long Night will bring him to the Duel-ender, and he means to call her to blood there for Corwen.
The footing stones of the Long Walk's last span were carted off over the winter for the new reef wall of a Tide House compound.

In spring a fighter from the Carter's Rest ladder, with a black cord knotted with salt-white twine on his hilt, was rowed over to the Reefhold platform for a single bout, lost it in the first exchange, and was rowed back the same night.

Jory Fenwick swapped Dace Orrin's bout blade for one with a cracked tang on the night before Dace's challenge; it broke in the first exchange and laid Dace's forearm open. Jory is deep in debt to a Saltmarket moneylender, and someone has been paying it down.
Dace Orrin's broken bout was his challenge for the Carter's Rest Fourth Rung; by the ladder's rule its holder keeps the rung on a forfeit, as he has twice since spring.
Haskel Brin was at the Spoke and Kettle mending harness for a carters' train the whole evening the blade was swapped; the train's driver will say so.
Senna Brook's own challenge for the Fourth Rung was drawn for after Dace's, so a forfeit by Dace did her no good.
Eighteen winters ago, before he joined the Society, Osgar Holt killed Edda Rusk in a tavern-yard duel at Highcrossing.
Osgar Holt and Talia Venn have sworn under Society rules, before Nessa Pryde, to a first-touch bout for Osgar's Second Rung.
Hollis Wray, Edda Rusk's son, has come to every one of Osgar's bouts for eighteen years. He wants to see Osgar hold a blow he could have landed, and has never said so.

Nessa Pryde chalks every Long Night on her yard wall: eleven bouts since the first, all against the Carter's Rest Fourth Rung, none bloodied. This year's line reads 'Carter's Rest: held since spring by the same man.'
By a handshake twelve years old, the Society's ring has the Gull and Barrel yard on bout nights.

As Sefton Gale witnessed it, the handshake gave the ring the yard on bout nights 'for as long as the Barrel stands' and said nothing of other lets. Wenna Cobb broke no word letting the yard to the haulers on other nights, but she has let them have bout nights too.
The harbour works have marked the yard's back wall and half its floor to come down for the new quay road this summer.

On the Gull and Barrel yard's oldest post hangs a black cord knotted with salt-white twine, Saltmarket's mourning knot for a fighter who died in a ring, nailed up twelve winters ago. This spring someone tied a fresh one beside it.

Jory Fenwick paid two carters to take the grey-bearded guest from the Spoke and Kettle's back room out to a shepherd's hut on the Wainyard road and keep him there past the Long Night draw. He meant Abner Quill, the Ring's old chalk-master, who had come to watch the Fourth Rung and knew Corwen's second by sight. The carters took Ruel Ambry, who had the room that night.
Pim Lowry, who argued with Ruel Ambry over a fare, was on the Lanternhall road with a load that night; the Lanternhall gate saw him.

Brannoc Teale, his name out, has gone over to the old-school yards. With Aldous Kett and a band of Saltmarket blades he has taken the Four Ways challenge stone, hung a purse on it for any Society fighter who will answer, and by the stone's old rule called out every Society fighter on the Carter Roads on blood terms. The Society's circuit has stopped running the Carter Roads.

At the Carter's Rest ladder reading, Brannoc Teale swore before the yard that Hesper Doane knew who he was when she signed him, sold him the Fourth Rung for a keeper's share of the Long Night purse, and bid him throw every bout he threw. Liʻo has stood Hesper down from the ladder until the Ring rules on it.
Hesper Doane is stood down from the Carter's Rest ladder, accused under the code of selling a rung.

Brannoc Teale's people have chalked the first Long Night on every challenge stone of the Carter Roads and the Harbour Coast: Corwen Ashgrove's name, Kitim's, and 'nobody dies'. At the Ring, before the morning crowd, Brannoc called Kitim Duel-ender out on blood terms, and she took the call.
Wren owes the circuit her season's entry fees, and the purse hung on the Four Ways stone would clear them. She has told no one.
The blades took Ennis Coombe off the Carter Road because he has sparred the Duel-ender twice a week for six years; they need him to teach Brannoc her guard.
Ennis Coombe is one of the Society's deadly half: outside the ring he has never fought at less than full, and inside it he has never drawn blood.
Ennis could slip the fold any night. He stays because he is teaching Brannoc to hold a blow, and believes nobody else will.
Aldous Kett held the line at the Crownsgate rout in the last imperial war, where the sword-school boys who had only ever fought for points died in the first hour.
Whoever keeps the Four Ways stone keeps its call-days and its old rule: anyone may call out a member here.
Hesper Doane and Aldous Kett have sworn before Jonah Thresh, at the stone, that a first-touch bout on the call-day decides who keeps the Four Ways stone.

Mirela Dunn, Corwen Ashgrove's widow, has sent word by Aldous Kett: she wants no more blood spent on Corwen's name and will stand with Hesper Doane against it. Her price: the Ring pays Corwen's household the first Long Night purse it kept.

After Brannoc's oath, the Fourth Rung bettors swore to the road-warden that the Carter's Rest chalk was false, and Mattias Stroud locked the ladder's chalk-keeper and her pot-boy in the Four Ways waystation for forging results under the road's law.
Linnet Crale chalked only the results the ring-keeper called. Nothing on the Carter's Rest board was false.
Jory Fenwick kept the bout-book on the Fourth Rung bouts at the circuit's fairs and paid out on every bout Wil Marrow threw; the bettors who backed Marrow lost to him.
Jory's winnings from the book went into the purse hung on the Four Ways stone.
Hesper never knew Wil Marrow was Brannoc Teale. The 'ladder card in her hand' Brannoc showed the yard is the results card she signs for every rung change, and she took nothing for it.
Hesper Doane stood as Kitim's second at the first Long Night, the night Corwen Ashgrove died, and has stood second to her at every Long Night since.
Kitim Duel-ender and Brannoc Teale have sworn at the Ring's chalk line, before Liʻo, to abide by the Long Night bout on blood terms.

What Brannoc wants is for the Duel-ender to name Corwen before the Long Night crowd as the man the Ring was built on, and for the Ring to pay his household the first purse. He has told Mirela that if he gets neither he does not mean to walk out of the Ring.
